segments.text: AI builds an answer one token at a time.
At each step, the model calculates probabilities for the tokens that could come next,
but AI doesn't always pick the highest probability token
to understand why we'll look at two things, sampling and temperature.
Let's say you ask, what should I name my new dog?
The AI builds the reply up to a frozen context.
You could name him, leaving a blank space for the very next choice.
At this exact blank, the AI calculates a probability for every token in its vocabulary.
Spot emerges as the leading choice at 22%.
Because Spot is the top choice at 22%, you might expect the AI to pick it every time.
But having the best chance doesn't mean a 100% win rate.
A 22% probability means AI would pick Spot about 22 times out of 100 tries,
on average, if the odds stay the same.
That's called sampling.
This chart shows exactly how this works in practice.
We are going to keep the 22% probability for Spot
and all the other odds completely unchanged
to see how sampling plays out across five random picks for this same open token.
These five random picks produce pick one, Max, pick two, Spot, pick three, Buddy,
pick four, Rex and pick five, Max.
These are not five names in a row in a single sentence.
They are five separate parallel attempts at filling that exact same single blank.
Notice that despite having the highest probability, Spot was only picked once.
Another set of five picks could turn out entirely differently.
The highest statistical chance is not a strict guarantee.
If an AI simply chose the most likely token every single time,
the resulting answers would become highly predictable and repetitive.
Giving other likely tokens, like Max or Buddy, a chance to be selected,
introduces necessary variety into the responses.
Each token the AI chooses shapes the permanent context for the very next choice,
creating a cascading effect.
One slightly different token choice at a critical juncture
can send the entire remainder of the generated answer in a completely new direction.
Temperature is the tool that changes how concentrated or spread out these probabilities are.
In chat apps, it's already set for you behind the scenes.
This table compares next token probabilities under different settings.
Looking at the baseline odds calculated from the model's training
and the frozen prompt context, we see Spot starts at 22%.
Watch what happens when we lower the temperature.
A lower temperature concentrates the odds heavily onto the most likely tokens.
Spot's chance leaps from 22% to 36%,
which effectively shrinks the chances for the less likely names.
A higher temperature does the exact reverse, spreading the odds more widely across the vocabulary.
Here, Spot's dominant chance falls to just 16%.
This levels the playing field, giving less likely names a much better chance of being picked.
Comparing Spot's isolated trajectory across all three environments
cements the concept.
A 22% baseline to start, up to 36% with low temperature
and down to 16% with high temperature.
The other category comprises the vast remainder of the vocabulary.
This demonstrates how temperature dynamically reshapes the entirety of the selection pool
in a fraction of a second.
Temperature reshapes the probabilities used to pick the next token.
It doesn't change what the model learned.
Adjusting temperature and utilizing sampling are purely selection mechanics.
The underlying intelligence and training weights of the model remain completely untouched.
As we have seen, the best chance isn't a guarantee.
Different choices, same learned weights.
